title: TA7-01729
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the claimant) is a female citizen of St. Vincent. She fears that her father will persecute her if she returns to St. Vincent. Given the circumstances of this claim, I have taken into consideration the Gender Guidelines1 in assessing this claim. Allegations
The clamant made the following allegations in the narrative of her Personal Information Form (PIF).2

The claimant's father began abusing her when she was 12 years old. He verbally and physically abused the claimant as well as her mother and her sisters. The claimant did not report her father's abuse to the police because it went against the teachings of her church and because the few police officers on the island of XXXXX, where the claimant and her family lived, would not stop her father from beating or abusing her. The claimant's sister XXXXX reported her father to the police and, as a result, her father attacked XXXXX. Two of the claimant's other sisters ran away because of her father's abuse. The claimant began living with friends and family at age 15 or 16 and got a job to support herself.

The claimant's father continues to abuse the claimant's mother and younger sister. The claimant cannot return to St. Vincent and live on any island other than XXXXX because all of her family lives on XXXXX.

The claimant initially filed a Humanitarian and Compassionate application for permanent residence upon the advice of a consultant. After paying him and waiting for a "long time", the claimant realized the consultant did nothing to assist the claimant. The claimant then made a claim for refugee protection. Analysis

The claimant's claim is, essentially, that her father was verbally and physically abusive to her and other family members and the claimant fears that her father will resume his abuse of her if she returns to St. Vincent. I find that the claimant's allegations about her father's ongoing verbal and physical abuse of herself and other family members is not credible due to a significant omission in her testimony for which she did not provide a reasonable explanation. Specifically, the claimant omitted that she was verbally or physically assaulted by her father from the statement she wrote during the "in-person refugee intake" appointment at the Citizenship and Immigration Canada offices in Etobicoke when she initiated her claim for refugee protection (hereinafter "CIC statement").3 I also find that the documents (letters) submitted by the claimant in support of her allegations of abuse to be fraudulent.4

In answer to question #3c of the Schedule 1 Background Information Form, which asks, "what are you afraid of if you returned to your country?" the claimant wrote "am afraid of my drunkie father."5 In response to question #3d in the same form, which asks, "whom are you afraid of if you returned to your country?" the claimant responded "Doctor."6 The claimant prepared a two-page written statement at the Citizenship and Immigration. On the first page of this statement, the claimant stated that her father is always drunk and sometimes falls over or walks on (steps on) family members sleeping in the living room or makes them sleep outside the house. The claimant states that she sometimes slept outside because she was ill. The claimant also stated that her father could not afford shoes for all the children in the family and could not afford to send them all to school at once. On the second page of her statement, the claimant wrote that she is asthmatic and was very ill in St. Vincent. She stated that the medical care she received in St. Vincent was poor and the medical care in Canada is much better.

In summation, the claimant indicated that, due to her father's drunkenness, there was physical upheaval in the household, there were hardships for the family due to poverty and she was ill from asthma and unable to get proper treatment. However, the claimant omitted from her two-page CIC statement any particular reference to her father purposely and physically assaulting her or verbally abusing her.

In her narrative, the claimant stated that her father physically abused her, in particular, that he "struck," "slapped," "kicked," and "whipped" her.7 The claimant also stated in her narrative that her father verbally abused her, sometimes calling her offensive names publicly. The claimant stated that her father also "attacked" her sister XXXXX and that her mother cries because of her father's continuing "abuse and violence."

I find that the claimant's account, in her CIC statement, of her father falling down and "walking on" herself and other family members indicates that this behaviour was a result of her father's drunkenness combined with sleeping arrangements that had some family members sleeping on the living room floor due to a lack of beds and space in the house. I find that this is not an example of the claimant's father physically assaulting her. Instead, I find that it is an example of the unfortunate consequence of her father's addiction and her family's poverty. I also find that the claimant's account of her father sometimes forcing family members to sleep outside indicates these incident were also as a result of his drunkenness and the lack of space in the house. While the latter type of behaviour can be considered abusive (as much psychologically as physically), the claimant indicated that the reason she sometimes slept outside was due to her illness (asthma) and not because her father forced her to do so.

The claimant provided two different explanations for omitting from her CIC statement any mention of her father physically and verbally assaulting her. Initially, the claimant explained that there was "no reason" she failed to indicate, in her CIC statement, that her father physically and verbally assaulted her. The claimant offered another explanation for the omission, specifically, that she was told that she could fill in the rest of her statement when she got a lawyer. I find that, if fear of abuse by her father was the main reason for her claim for refugee protection, being advised that she would have an opportunity to fill in or amplify her statement with her lawyer does not explain why the claimant did not make any reference to physical or verbal assaults directed at her by her father in her CIC statement. The claimant wrote an approximately 200-word paragraph about her father's behaviour and actions in her CIC statement and she had ample opportunity, while writing this statement, to include some reference to verbal or physical abuse such as "striking," "slapping," "kicking," or "whipping" which are the terms she used in her narrative. The claimant did not use any of these words or even more general terms such as "beat," "abuse" or "attack" to describe her father's treatment of her. I find that, had the claimant suffered verbal and physical assaults directed at her by her father as she described in her narrative, it is reasonable to expect that she would have included at least some small reference to these serious and relevant incidents in her CIC statement and would not have completely omitted such reference because she was advised she could provide further information once she had a lawyer.

In assessing the claimant's credibility, I note that the claimant completed nine years of education in St. Vincent. The interview at CIC was conducted in English and the written forms were completed in English, the claimant's mother tongue. There was no evidence presented indicating that the claimant had any cognitive difficulties or low intellectual functioning. I have taken into account that victims of domestic and family violence may have difficulty clearly recalling past incidents when providing testimony.8 However, in this case, the claimant did not simply provide inconsistent, vague or incomplete testimony about physical and verbal abuse by her father in the written CIC statement but, rather, she completely omitted any reference to such treatment from her father.

Therefore, I find that the claimant would have realized that, had she experienced incidents of physical and verbal assaults by her father, in addition to experiencing the ongoing hardships resulting from her father's alcoholism and the family's poverty, it would have been important to make at least some reference to the more serious incidents of assaults in her statement at CIC rather than wait to mention these until she had a lawyer.

Due to the omission of references to verbal and physical abuse in the CIC statement, in the absence of a reasonable explanation for this omission, I find the claimant's later testimony in her narrative and in oral testimony about abuse by her father to be not credible.

I also draw a negative inference with respect to the credibility of the claimant's testimony about being abused by her father due to the letters she provided in Exhibit C-4 to support her claim. The claimant presented four letters: the letters were ostensibly signed by four family members, specifically, her three sisters and her mother. I find that these are fraudulent documents fabricated by the claimant in an attempt to bolster her claim for refugee protection for the following reasons.

When the handwriting (printing) in each of these four letters is compared to that in each of the other letters, it appears to be practically identical. When the handwriting (printing) in these letters is compared to the claimant's own handwriting (printing) in the CIC statement, it appears to be practically identical (with the exception of one paragraph that is printed with more of a forehand slant than the rest).

The claimant indicated that her sisters, XXXXX and XXXXX, wrote the four letters, in effect penning the letters for the claimant's sister XXXXX and her mother XXXXX, in addition to writing their own letters. When asked why XXXXX and XXXXX would not have signed the letters they wrote on behalf of their other family members to reflect this reality, the claimant did not provide an explanation. The claimant indicated that she, XXXXX and XXXXX all went to the same school and, thus, they all had similar handwriting. I take judicial notice that, after leaving school, over time, people's handwriting (printing) becomes more differentiated from the style of script they are taught to model in school and, while family members may display some common handwriting or printing traits, mature adults usually have distinguishable handwriting (printing) styles. Thus, I find that even if the three sisters (the claimant, XXXXX and XXXXX) went to the same school and were trained in the same style of handwriting (printing), given that XXXXX is now approximately 29 years old and the claimant is approximately 31 years old, their handwriting would have evolved from the style they were taught in school. I find it implausible that the claimant, XXXXX and XXXXX would currently have practically identical handwriting styles. Thus, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant wrote the four letters contained in Exhibit C-4 as the handwriting in those four letters matches the handwriting in the claimant's CIC statement. I therefore do not rely on the contents of these letters to be trustworthy evidence that the claimant was abused by her father or that other family members suffered similar abuse as that alleged by the claimant.

In addition, I draw a negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility in general due to her attempt to bolster her refugee claim with these fraudulent documents. The claimant did not provide any other independent documentary evidence corroborating her claim such as a report from the police about her sister XXXXX making a denunciation about the claimant's father; a letter from a community or church leader who could have been aware of the alleged situation between the claimant and her father; or medical reports regarding injuries from having been slapped, kicked, or whipped by her father which, had those injuries existed, presumably would have been noticed by the doctors treating the claimant for asthma.

The significant omission from the CIC statement and the fraudulent documents both pertain directly to the central aspect of the claimant's claim for refugee protection, specifically, abuse by her father which she claims to fear would resume if she returns to St Vincent. Given this omission and the fraudulent documents, I find that the claimant's written testimony in her narrative and her oral testimony regarding being verbally and physically abused by her father is not credible. Thus, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the claimant was not verbally or physically assaulted and therefore these allegations do not contribute to establishing an objective basis for the claimant's fear of persecution by her father if she returns to St. Vincent. Though the claimant's home life, when growing up, might have been unsettled and difficult due to her father's drunkenness and physically uncomfortable due to poverty, these circumstances do not amount to persecution. Moreover, given that the claimant is an adult who would not need to return to her family's home if she returned to St. Vincent, the claimant would not be impacted by these conditions now as she was in her childhood. Conclusion

Accordingly, the panel finds that there is not a serious possibility that the claimant will be persecuted by her father if she returns to St. Vincent. The claimant did not provide any evidence that she fears persecution by anyone else in St. Vincent, aside from her father. She also did not provide any evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, she would be personally subjected to a risk to her life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture if she returns to St. Vincent.

Hence, the Refugee Protection Division determines that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection and rejects her claim for refugee protection.
